opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the long-term vision is really that this becomes something people just expect, the way you'd expect an energy label on a fridge or a washing machine. Right now, when someone picks a model, whether it's a developer choosing what to deploy or a company deciding which API to call, they look at accuracy, maybe latency, maybe cost. But energy is almost never part of that conversation, mostly because the information just isn't there. So the first goal is to make that information exist and be comparable.

What we've done so far is set up a standardized way of testing models on a fixed set of tasks, things like text generation, summarization, image generation, classification, on the same hardware, and then measuring how much energy they use for inference. Then we give them a relative rating, kind of a star system, within each task category. Comparing a small classification model to a huge image generation model doesn't really make sense, but comparing two summarization models does.

Long term, I'd love to see a few things. One is broader participation, especially from the companies building closed models. Right now it's much easier for us to evaluate open models because we can run them ourselves. For proprietary models we need those companies to either submit their models or run the benchmark themselves in a way we can verify. I'm hoping that as there's more pressure, from users and from regulation, that becomes the norm.

On that note, I think policy is a big piece. In Europe, with the AI Act, there's already language around energy reporting and transparency, and I'd love for something like this to become the practical tool regulators point to. You can't regulate what you can't measure, so having a common methodology matters a lot.

And then the other thing is keeping it alive and evolving. AI moves really fast, so the tasks, the hardware, the models all change. It can't be a one-off leaderboard that goes stale. It has to be updated regularly, and it has to cover new things like agentic workflows or reasoning models, which use a lot more compute per query.

Ultimately what I want is for people to be able to make an informed choice. Not everyone needs the biggest model for every task. If you knew a model ten times smaller did your task just as well and used a fraction of the energy, a lot of people would make that choice. We just need to give them the information.

r001.rationale: The response describes the work so far as a standardized method for testing models, measuring inference energy, and assigning comparable ratings, framing it as the start of a system people will come to expect.

r002.rationale: It says the system must be updated regularly as AI changes and cover emerging tasks and models, including agentic workflows and reasoning models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the long-term vision is really that it becomes something people don't have to think about, the same way you don't think about the Energy Star sticker on a fridge until you're actually standing in the store comparing two of them. Right now, if you want to know how much energy a model uses, you basically have to be me. You have to go run the model yourself, measure it, and that's not realistic for most developers, let alone for companies or policymakers.

So the first phase, which is where we are now, is building out the methodology and the leaderboard. We take a bunch of open models, we run them on a standardized set of tasks, same hardware, same number of queries, and we measure the energy. And then we rate them, one to five stars, where five stars is the most efficient in its category. That's the Energy Star part. It's deliberately simple, because the whole point is that a star rating is something you can put on a model card or in a dropdown menu, and people get it immediately.

Where I want this to go is a couple of directions. One is that it becomes a default thing on platforms. If you're on the Hub, or any model hub really, and you're picking between models, you see the energy rating right next to the accuracy numbers. Because today we optimize entirely for performance on benchmarks, and energy is just invisible. I want it to be a first-class axis, so people start making that tradeoff consciously. Do I actually need the biggest model for this task, or is the three-star one that uses a tenth of the energy good enough?

The second direction is the closed models. That's the hard part. We can't measure what we can't run, and the big API providers aren't disclosing anything. So in the longer term I'd love to see this become something that companies report, either voluntarily because there's demand from customers, or because regulators start asking for it. The EU AI Act already has some language about energy reporting, and having a concrete, standardized methodology that already exists makes it a lot easier for regulators to say, okay, do this. That's actually a big part of why we built it the way we did, so there's something ready to go.

And then honestly, the dream is that it influences how models get built, not just how they get chosen. If efficiency becomes something you get credit for, something that shows up on a leaderboard people care about, then you get a feedback loop. Labs start competing on it. We've seen that happen with everything else we benchmark, for better or worse, so why not use that dynamic for something that actually helps.

I don't think it'll look exactly like what we have today. The categories will change, the tasks will change, the hardware will change. But the core idea, that you should be able to glance at a model and know roughly what it costs to run, in energy terms, I think that's going to be necessary. The scale we're operating at now, you can't keep treating it as an afterthought.

r001.rationale: It describes the current phase as building a methodology and leaderboard that measure open models under standardized tasks and assign energy stars, presenting that work as the first step toward broader ratings.

r002.rationale: It says the categories, tasks, and hardware will change, but does not clearly say the system will evolve as new models emerge.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that it becomes something people can actually use when choosing a model. With an Energy Star label, you don’t have to understand all the engineering inside an appliance to get a sense of how efficient it is. I’d love for us to have something similar for AI, where energy use is visible alongside performance, so people can make an informed choice about what they need.

Long term, I’d like that to create an incentive for developers to make models more efficient, too. But we need a fair way to compare them, because different models do different things, and the way you run a model matters. So I see the rating as a starting point for making energy efficiency a routine part of how we evaluate AI.

r001.rationale: The response calls the rating a starting point and says comparisons should be fair, but does not identify it as a research proof of concept or clearly describe a standardized rating system.

r002.rationale: It notes that models do different things and execution affects comparisons, but does not say the rating will evolve as new tasks and models emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
My hope is that it becomes something people can use when they’re choosing a model, the same way they might look at an Energy Star label when buying an appliance. Right now, it’s quite hard to understand the energy implications of using one model versus another. I’d love to make that information accessible and comparable.

Long term, I’d like to see energy efficiency become a standard part of how we evaluate models, alongside accuracy and other capabilities. That doesn’t mean everybody needs to use the smallest model for everything. It means being able to choose a model that does your task well without consuming more energy than necessary. And hopefully, making that visible also gives developers an incentive to build more efficient models.

r001.rationale: The response calls for energy efficiency to become a standard part of model evaluation, but does not identify Luccioni’s research proof of concept or frame it as a step toward that system.
